text: This chapter has built up identity, continuous evaluation, and device compliance as three signals in one access decision. This final lesson is the synthesis: putting PIM, Conditional Access, and AWS IAM roles together into one coherent identity fabric for an org that runs Azure and AWS side by side, rather than treating each cloud as its own island.

The problem it solves is the identity silo. An org can end up, almost by accident, with Entra ID governing Azure while a completely separate set of AWS IAM users and access keys governs AWS, created independently with no relationship between the two. That's two perimeters pretending to be one. A user disabled in Entra ID the instant they leave the company can still hold working AWS access keys for weeks, because nothing connects the two systems' idea of who should have access.

The fix is federation. AWS IAM Identity Center, the successor to AWS SSO, federates sign-in to an external identity provider over SAML, so a user never gets a separate AWS username and password — they sign in through Entra ID and get mapped to permission sets in the target AWS account. Because that sign-in goes through Entra ID, it's subject to the exact same Conditional Access policy as everything else: the same device compliance check, the same risk evaluation, and the same continuous access evaluation, so a disabled or high-risk account loses its path into AWS too.

Once a federated identity lands in AWS, it doesn't get standing permissions either. Access is granted through temporary credentials issued by AWS's Security Token Service, tied to an assumed role with a defined, limited lifetime. Line that up against PIM: eligible, then activated with justification and often approval, then time-boxed before it expires. Different cloud, same underlying principle — privilege is borrowed for a bounded window, not held indefinitely.

Put together, the fabric is one identity source of truth in Entra ID, one policy decision point in Conditional Access that every sign-in passes through across Microsoft 365, Azure, and federated AWS alike, continuous access evaluation keeping that decision fresh through the session, and time-boxed elevation on both sides — PIM in Azure, STS-issued temporary credentials in AWS.

A capstone-level review isn't about naming all three pieces — it's tracing one access request end to end and showing there's no silent gap where a disabled account, a non-compliant device, or an expired elevation could still reach something, in either cloud. Chapter 3 picks up from here, moving from verifying identity to limiting what a verified identity can actually reach.
